newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM hopeful vows stable economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM hopeful vows stable economic growth.

text.p: Thai prime minister hopeful Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said on Thursday if elected he would bring in a qualified economic team and stress disciplined monetary policy.

Chavalit, a former defence minister whose New Aspiration Party (NAP) seeks to win enough parliamentary seats in a general election next month to lead the government, also dismissed a public perception that he would advocate big military spending.

Chavalit and his economic advisors told foreign businessmen through teleconferences that he would seek to promote Thailand's long-term economic and monetary stability if elected to succeed his rival, Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa.

"Investor confidence was in the past influenced by inflation but recently it was affected by qualifications of economic ministers. We will stress the choosing of qualified and honest people (to serve in the cabinet)," he said.

Chavalit, whose NAP hopes to win at least 130 of 393 seats in the lower House of Representatives, was referring to the failure of Banharn's economic team to win the support of private business and market investors over the past 14 months.

Analysts said Chavalit's teleconferences with a small group of businessmen in Hong Kong, Singapore and London aimed to shore up the image of the NAP, which some say lacks a good economic team compared with its close rival, the Democrat Party of former prime minister Chuan Leekpai.
The former army chief said "...fiscal and monetary policies must be disciplined and budget must be balanced".

His economic advisor Surasak Nananukool said a Chavalit-led coalition would help small and medium-sized business by cutting bureaucratic red tape, reducing utility charges and speeding up the process for them to reclaim a seven percent value added tax.

Surasak said a government led by the retired army general would maintain the stability of the Thai baht. "We don't want to interfere with the Bank of Thailand and the finance ministry. They've good people to handle the job."

The economist said Thailand's high current account deficit of about 8.1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) could be curbed by raising household savings, increasing provident fund contributions of company employees to 15 percent from five and restructuring export industries that are losing competitiveness to Thai neighbours.
The Thai GDP is projected to grow at a 10-year low of less than seven percent this year.
